sections.h2: What makes selling in West New York different
sections.html:
West New York packs more than 53,000 people into a single square mile on the Hudson Palisades, and a transfer here goes through a town inspection before the deed moves. Roughly three of every four households rent, so the people who bid on a two- or three-family building are often landlords weighing rent rolls.

The sections below cover the town's housing figures, transit, the ownership certificate rules, tax payment habits and the county office that records deeds.

The town has 53,192 residents on 0.99 square miles of land, between Guttenberg, North Bergen, Union City, Weehawken and the river.

A bilingual listing and a bilingual contact for showings widen your audience here. Rent of $1,716 beside owner costs above $3,000 a month explains why investors price a small building by its rental income.

Bergenline Avenue, home to over 300 shops and restaurants, is the commercial spine, while 60th Street is the main crosstown road and the site of Town Hall. County Route 501 follows Kennedy Boulevard along the west edge and County Route 505 follows Boulevard East, so no state highway enters the town. The Turnpike, Route 1/9 and Route 495 sit in adjacent municipalities.

  • NJ Transit buses 128, 154, 156, 158, 159, 165, 166 and 168 reach Midtown's Port Authority Bus Terminal, and routes 181 and 188 go to the George Washington Bridge Bus Terminal.
  • The Hudson-Bergen Light Rail stops at Bergenline Avenue on the Union City line, and the Port Imperial ferry terminal is in Weehawken.
  • Jitneys along Bergenline Avenue can arrive as often as once a minute.

North Hudson Regional Fire and Rescue protects the town in place of a local fire department. Newark Liberty International Airport is 13.6 miles away, and LaGuardia is 13.5 miles away through the Lincoln Tunnel.

Chapter 148 of the town code bars anyone from selling a residential building, or taking title to one, until the town issues an ownership certificate following an inspection. The rule reaches one-, two- and three-family homes, buildings of four or more units, commercial and mixed-use buildings, and vacant land through a separate certificate. A missed certificate brings a $1,000 fine.

  • Seller or buyer may file the application, and both carry liability if none is obtained.
  • When the contract calls for an as-is sale, a copy goes in with the application, signed by both parties.
  • Inspectors look at housing, building, fire, electrical and property maintenance codes.
  • If repairs will not be finished by closing, the town can grant a temporary certificate lasting up to six months with no renewal, and the buyer takes on the duty to correct the violations.

State fire rules separately ask for an alarm certificate covering smoke and carbon monoxide detectors when a house of one or two units is sold, so ask the town which office issues it and book both visits once you have a signed contract.

sections.h2: Selling a building with open violations
sections.html:
An as-is sale is common here, and the temporary certificate is what makes it workable. The buyer agrees in writing to correct the violations within the six months, and the town decides which items qualify. Put the as-is language in the contract, have both parties sign the copy that goes with the application, and keep a record of every item the inspector lists.

If you are a landlord with tenants in the building, ask your attorney how the inspection fits around the leases. Access dates, notice to tenants and who pays for corrections are the points that usually cause friction, and settling them before the application goes in keeps the schedule intact.

sections.h2: Property tax payments and tax sales
sections.html:
The Tax Collector bills and collects municipal property taxes from the office at 428 60th Street, and the phone line is 201-295-5110. A ten-day grace period applies. Interest is counted from the original due date starting on day eleven, and a postmark does not count as payment.

The town holds its tax sale in December and announces the date by the end of November. Owners with a balance should request a payoff figure before listing so a lien can be cleared out of the proceeds.

sections.h2: Deed recording and the state fee
sections.html:
The Hudson County Register records the deed, not Town Hall. Paper filings need the county cover sheet, checks go to Hudson County Register, and a personal or LLC check cannot exceed $200. Questions can go to 201-395-4760.

The seller pays New Jersey's realty transfer fee on the price. A slice of a sale between $200,000 and $550,000 costs $4.80 per $500, which is where a typical West New York price falls, and anything above $1 million adds the Graduated Percent Fee. The closing statement shows the total.

sections.h2: How to sell a West New York property
sections.html:
Owners here usually weigh a listing, a private deal and a direct purchase for cash, and the town certificate applies to every one of them.

  • A listing fits a house or unit in good order that a lender can appraise, with the inspection and loan timeline that follows.
  • A private deal works when a tenant, relative or neighbor is already the buyer and a lawyer drafts the contract.
  • A cash purchase can fit a building with open violations, a tenancy you no longer want to run, or an estate that needs to close.

Write down who pays for certificate inspection and corrections before you sign anything.

sections.h2: Order of steps for a seller
sections.html:
Begin with the Tax Collector, since a payoff figure tells you what a lien or balance will take from the proceeds. Next, decide who will file the ownership certificate application, you or the buyer, and agree that in the contract. Once the contract is signed, book the town inspection and the alarm certificate visit together so the building is only opened to inspectors once.

Then give your attorney the deed, the county cover sheet requirements and the transfer fee estimate so the filing with the Hudson County Register is ready on closing day. A cash buyer can shorten the wait for financing, but the certificate and the recording still set the earliest closing date. Ask the buyer for proof of funds and a written closing date, and compare offers by what you keep after taxes, the state fee and any repairs the buyer wants you to cover.

faqs.q: Is an inspection required before a West New York sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Under Chapter 148 an ownership certificate must be issued after inspection before a residential building transfers. Skipping it costs $1,000, and the seller and the buyer are both responsible.

faqs.q: Can I sell a West New York building with open violations?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The town may grant a temporary certificate for up to six months when violations remain at closing, and the buyer agrees to fix them. The Department of Public Affairs decides which items qualify.

faqs.q: How long is the West New York property tax grace period?
faqs.a: Ten days. Interest is charged back to the due date beginning on the eleventh day, and postmarks do not count. The Tax Collector at 201-295-5110 can give you a current balance.

faqs.q: Which office records a West New York deed?
faqs.a: The Hudson County Register. File with the county's cover sheet and a check made out to Hudson County Register, which your closing attorney or title agent normally arranges.

faqs.q: Do most West New York residents own their homes?
faqs.a: No. Only 23.0 percent of occupied homes are owned by the people living in them, and median gross rent is $1,716, so many buyers are investors who weigh rental income.
